title: The Lesson I Learned From Peter’s Restoration — John 21:15
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Peter’s Restoration — John 21:15
He did not start with Peter’s failure.
He started with love.

After the denial.
After the shame.
After the rooster cried and Peter’s heart broke under the weight of his own weakness.
Jesus looked at the man who fell the hardest and asked one piercing question: “Do you love Me?” (John 21:15)

Not, “Why did you fail Me?”
Not, “Can I trust you again?”
Not, “Explain yourself.”
Just this.
Do you love Me?
That wrecks me.

Because when I read Peter’s restoration, I see that Jesus is not only interested in exposing sin. He is committed to restoring souls. Peter had publicly denied Christ three times, and now Jesus lovingly walks him back through grace, one question at a time. Not to humiliate him. To heal him.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Some of us think our loudest failure is the end of our calling. But John 21 says otherwise. Jesus did not discard Peter. He restored him, recommissioned him, and trusted him again with, “Feed My lambs.” Grace did not ignore Peter’s sin. Grace met Peter in it, brought repentance through love, and then gave him purpose again.
Here’s the lesson:
Your worst moment does not get the final word when Jesus is in the story.

Peter’s fall was real.
His tears were real.
His repentance was real.
And Christ’s mercy was more real still.

Maybe you failed God in the very place where you promised you never would.
Maybe shame has been preaching louder than Scripture.
Maybe you still love Jesus, but you are crushed by how badly you have stumbled.
Listen to me, beloved:

Jesus still comes to broken disciples.
Jesus still asks heart-level questions.
Jesus still restores people who thought they were finished.

The Gospel is not that faithful people never fail.
The Gospel is that Jesus saves, restores, and recommissions failing people who return to Him in repentance and love.

Peter’s story is our story.
Sin is real.
Repentance is necessary.
Grace is greater.
And Jesus is still calling wounded people back to the fire — not to destroy them, but to remake them.
Come back to Him.

Not with excuses.
Not with polished words.
Just with an honest heart.
“Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You.” (John 21:17)
That prayer still reaches heaven.
